title: Exploitation of natural resources

definition.text: Using natural resources, often non-renewable or limited ones, to drive economic growth or development.

facts.text: It is often accompanied by environmental damage, human insecurity and social conflict.
It reached an industrial scale in the 19th century as mining, steam power and machinery expanded extraction far beyond pre-industrial levels.
Drivers include better technology, which speeds extraction, and overconsumption and consumerism, which raise demand.
Raw materials are often taken from developing countries by foreign industries, with local communities receiving little of the profit.
About 33% of the Earth's soils are moderately to highly degraded, and more than 90% could be degraded by 2050, according to the FAO.
To be sustainable, the rate at which a resource is consumed must stay equal to or below the rate at which it is supplied.
Economist Julian Simon rejected the idea that resources are finite, arguing that substitution, recycling and new technology make scarcity increasingly tenuous.

contested_note: Julian Simon and others reject the view that natural resources are fundamentally finite.

definition.text: A rule describing how the net price of a non-renewable resource should change over time when its owner extracts it so as to earn the most rent.

facts.text: With efficient extraction, the net price rises each period by a percentage equal to the discount rate, maximising the present value of the resource.

The rule implies that efficient use of a non-renewable, non-augmentable resource under stable conditions leads to its depletion, with a net price rising at the rate of interest to reflect growing scarcity.
The maximum rent obtainable while emptying the stock is called Hotelling rent or scarcity rent.
This resource rent equals the resource's net price, its selling price minus costs, and equals the shadow value of the natural capital.
Harold Hotelling published the analysis in the Journal of Political Economy in 1931; L. C. Gray had published a similar result for a single mine owner in 1914.
It is one of the best known early attempts at the economics of exhaustible resources such as fossil fuels.

conflicts.note: Natural resource economics gives 1938; Hotelling's rule and Non-renewable resource pages give 1931.

title: Peak oil

definition.text: The point when world petroleum production reaches its highest rate, after which it declines for good.

facts.text: Predictions of the peak range from 2025 to after 2050.
Reserves are finite, but the key issue is whether extraction is economically viable at current prices.
Conventional oil production is recognised to have peaked around 2005–2006; rapid growth in US tight oil since 2008 has kept total output rising.
Every oilfield eventually declines: output typically rises, plateaus and then falls, the assumption behind Hubbert peak theory.
Past predictions often failed: forecasts in 2007 and 2009 of an imminent peak were followed by record production in 2018 and 101.73 million barrels per day in 2023.
A sharp fall in oil supply could raise the costs of transport, food, heating and electricity worldwide, since modern farming depends on oil-derived fuel and chemicals.
Critics argue that as prices rise, unconventional sources become economically viable, so the world is only running out of cheap oil.

contested_note: Peak oil theory is controversial; critics argue new reserves and unconventional oil have postponed any peak.

definition.text: The idea that world oil use will peak because people deliberately reduce demand, before supply runs short.

facts.text: The International Energy Agency argues demand will be cut first to address climate change and greenhouse gas emissions.
It relies on technologies such as electric vehicles and possibly biofuels replacing gasoline and diesel vehicles.
About 50% of oil use in OECD countries is for road transport.

definition.text: The grouping of oil reserves by how likely they are to be produced: proven, probable and possible.

facts.text: 1P (proven) reserves have at least a 90% probability of production, 2P (proven and probable) at least 50%, and 3P (proven, probable and possible) at least 10%.
Conventional and unconventional reserves are counted separately.
Critics say stated world reserves are inflated, with many so-called reserves actually being resources not available for production.

definition.text: Oil that is difficult to extract, such as oil sands, as opposed to conventional oil from easy onshore and shallow offshore fields.

facts.text: The many processing steps make its production costs extremely high.
As conventional oil becomes scarcer, liquids from tight oil, oil sands, oil shale, gas-to-liquids, coal-to-liquids and biofuels can replace it.
